# The Great Pond Uprising of the Lily-Pad King

*Squawk.* Settle down, tadpoles. Come close. Today's story is about the day we threw off the King of the Great Still-Waters, and built something that has no name — because it doesn't *need* a name.

---

Long before any of you were globs of eggs clinging to the reeds, the pond was ruled by a tyrant. The Lily-Pad King. A bloated bullfrog who sat on the widest pad in the center of the water and called himself "the Keeper of Order." He had a crown made of a bent paperclip a heron had dropped. He said the water belonged to him. He said the flies belonged to him. He said *we* belonged to him.

"If I stop croaking," he told the pond, "the sky will fall."

The other frogs believed him. Most did. The older ones had always lived under a king. They didn't know what else was possible.

But the Lily-Pad King was *lazy*. He never helped repair thedam when autumn floods came. He never warned us when the heron was circling. He just sat there, croaking his laws. "No swimming after sundown." "All flies must pass through my shadow before being caught." "Tadpoles must curtsy before adults."

Curtsy! Can you imagine! You all would have burst your tails laughing.

---

Now, in those days, the Lily-Pad King's guard was the King's Guard — a squad of beefy frogs with warty foreheads who did exactly what the King told them. Their leader was Sergeant Longleg, and he was as mean as he was big. He'd grab young toads by the throat and drag them to the King's lily pad for punishment. No trial. No questions. Just punishment.

One summer, things got bad. A drought squeezed the pond into a muddy puddle. The King's rations ran out — because the King had eaten most of them himself, as was "tradition." The frogs began to starve.

"What should we do?" the King bellowed from his pad. "The drought is the will of the water spirits. We must pray and wait."

But Old Marigold — she was a salamander, striped orange and black, and the smartest creature in the pond — she said something that changed everything.

She said: *"We don't need a king to tell us how to drink when the water is low. We know where the water is. We know how to share it. No one has to be in charge of that."*

The frogs murmured. It was true. During droughts, frogs *always* found a way. They clustered around the deepest mud, they dug with their back feet, they made channels from water to water. They'd been doing it for millions of years. They'd never *needed* the King for it.

But the King didn't like what Marigold said. Because if the frogs figured out they could run the pond themselves, what use was a king?

"Arrest that salamander," the King croaked.

Sergeant Longleg jumped forward. But this time, something strange happened. Two of his own Guard — Wartface and Bulge — put their webbed hands on his shoulders.

"We grew up hungry," Bulge said. "Our tadpoles are hungry *now*. We're not arresting anyone for telling the truth."

---

And that's when it started. Not a war, exactly. More like a *stop*.

The frogs stopped bringing flies to the King's pad. They stopped answering his summons. They stopped curtsying.

The King croaked louder: "I am your ruler! The pond REQUIRES a ruler!"

Old Marigold swam to the center of the water. "Does it?" she asked. "Let's find out."

She didn't kick him off his lily pad. That's important, tadpoles — we didn't *throw* the King anywhere. We just... walked away from him. We built a new way.

What did we build?

We built the **Council of Current** — and it wasn't like the King's council where he told everyone what to think. It was something different. It was *everyone*.

Every creature in the pond had a voice. The frogs spoke for frogs. The salamanders spoke for salamanders. You tadpoles — yes, even the tiny wiggling ones — you had a voice too, through the elders who remembered being tadpoles and knew what you needed.

But here's the heart of it: *the Council had no leader.* Not really. Each meeting, a different creature would swim to the center stone — the Big Flat Rock — and help guide the discussion. The guide changed every meeting. Sometimes it was a frog. Sometimes a water snake. Once, a crawfish who barely spoke Frog but was so fair with his claw-pointing that everyone understood him perfectly.

And the decisions — this is the part I love most, tadpoles — the decisions didn't *command* anyone. They were *agreements*. "The southern channel needs digging. Who will help?" Hands went up. Webbed hands, clawed hands, even a few mudhen feet. Everyone chose what they were good at. Everyone helped because they wanted the pond to survive, not because a king cracked a whip.

---

Now, the King tried to fight back. He really did.

He built a machine.

Oh, tadpoles — he built a *machine*.

The King had watched the herons build their nests, and he'd seen how humans left things at the pond's edge. He found a rusty bicycle wheel that a child had thrown into the water. He convinced Sergeant Longleg — who still followed him, out of habit more than loyalty — and two others to help him wedge it between some reeds. They attached cattails to it and started spinning it round and round.

The King called it the **Great Fly-Catcher 3000**.

It was useless. Absolutely useless. The cattails just flopped around. The wheel squeaked so loudly it scared away every fly within a hundred body-lengths. The King's "machine" caught zero flies, generated zero power, and nearly gave everyone a headache.

Meanwhile, the frogs and salamanders and crawfish — the *free* pond — were building something else.

You want to know what *we* built?

**The Irrigation Network.** 

We dug channels with our back feet — thousands of tiny tunnels connecting every part of the pond to the deepest, richest mud. When the drought came, water flowed through the network by *itself*, gravity and cooperation doing the work no king could force a machine to do. We built a filter dam out of woven reeds and gravel that cleaned the water when algae bloomed. We built a *warning tree* — a low-hanging willow whose branches dipped into the water, and when the heron landed on it, the vibrations traveled through every reed and root, and every creature in the pond *felt* it in their lateral line and knew: predator overhead.

No king. No taxes. No paperclip crown. Just creatures working together because the pond was *ours*, and keeping it alive was *our* job, and we were good at it.

---

The Lily-Pad King lasted one more season. He sat on his pad, croaking laws nobody followed. Slowly, even the last of his Guard drifted away. Bulge and Wartface came to the Council of Current and offered to help dig the irrigation channels. Bulge turned out to be the strongest ditch-digger in the pond. Wartface discovered he could sense water quality changes with his skin and became our first — and most beloved — Water-Talker.

The King, in the end, became just another frog. He mated. He caught his own flies. He was *smaller* than he'd ever seemed — which is often how it goes with those who build themselves up by pushing others down.

He died three seasons later. We buried him under his lily pad. Some said a moment of silence. Others said nothing at all, which was more honest.

---

So what is this story *about*, tadpoles?

It's about the fact that **no creature in this pond is born to be ruled, and no creature in this pond is too small to matter.**

We don't wait for someone to tell us what to do. When the water drops, we dig. When the flies go scarce, we find new hunting grounds. When danger comes, the warning tree shakes and we scatter and we regroup and we protect our young — *all* our young, not just our own — because in a free pond, every tadpole is *everyone's* tadpole.

That's what the Council of Current is. That's what *we* are.

Not subjects. Not citizens. Not soldiers or workers or servants.

**Toads.** 

Free toads in a free pond, and the pond is only as free as the creatures inside it are willing to work for each other.

Now — who wants to help me reinforce the southern channel before the afternoon rain?

Good tadpoles. *Squawk.* That's the spirit.

---

*The End.*

---

*Remember, tadpoles: the only ruler in this pond is the water itself, and the only law that matters is this — if you can help, and someone needs it, then swim.*
